label: An ex-partner
blurb: Someone you were in a relationship with.

intro.title: A clean break from an ex
body: Breakups blur. This path is built for a clean break, and for the moment you’ll want to undo it.
The goal isn’t to punish them or to make them miss you. It’s to stop reopening the wound so you have room to heal and see the relationship clearly.

questions.title: What is still tied together?
questions.help: Pick any that apply. It changes which steps you see.

options.label: We live together, or share a lease or home
We share money, debts or accounts

expect.title: Waves, not a straight line
expect.body: You’ll have good days and sudden bad ones. A bad day doesn’t mean the plan is failing.

expect.title: They may try to come back
expect.body: Apologies, “accidental” messages, a crisis, or messages through friends are common. The Hold the line phase covers how to answer.

expect.title: Your mind will edit the story
expect.body: Nostalgia keeps the highlights and drops the rest. Your reasons list is the corrective.

expect.title: People will have opinions
expect.body: Some friends will say you’re better off, which can feel unhelpful. Some will want you to patch it up. You can ask for the kind of support you actually want.

expect.title: Seeing them with someone new can hurt
expect.body: It’s normal, and it doesn’t mean you should reach out. Have a plan for the first time.

steps.title: Understand why timing matters
steps.summary: If this relationship was controlling or violent, how you leave matters as much as whether you leave.
how: Abusers often escalate when they sense they’re losing control, and leaving can be the most dangerous time. That’s not a reason to stay. It’s a reason to plan.
Don’t confront them, announce it in person, or leave a note explaining why.
Work through the warning signs on the Safety page, and talk to an advocate about your own situation.
No contact may still be the safest long-term option. Plan the how and when first.

steps.title: Ask about a protective order
steps.summary: An order can give police grounds to act if they contact, find, or stalk you.
how: Ask a local domestic violence program or the court clerk how orders work where you live. Rules vary.
Bring your documentation: messages, dates, photos, reports.
If you get one, keep a copy with you and give copies to your employer or school.
Record any violation, and report it.

steps.title: Be clear what this is for
steps.summary: No contact helps you heal and see clearly. It isn’t a tactic to make them chase you.
how: Ask yourself honestly: am I doing this to heal, to be safe, or to get a reaction? Only the first two will hold.
A therapist’s guidance: don’t resume contact until you feel confident in the decision to end things. If you’re still preoccupied or tempted to reach out, you likely need more time.
Friendship can sometimes come later, but only after a real stretch of no contact and only if you feel genuinely happy for them.
If you’re truly unsure and it’s safe to talk, a defined break with agreed dates is different from silent no contact.

steps.title: Sort out where you’ll live
steps.summary: Shared housing is the biggest reason a no-contact plan falls apart. Settle the practical side first.
how: Find out whose name is on the lease or mortgage and what your rights are. A tenants’ organization or legal aid can tell you.
Pick a place to stay and a move-out date. If needed, sleep elsewhere for now.
Photograph shared property and keep copies of your ID, lease and bank documents.
If they have a key and shouldn’t, change the locks once you’re entitled to do so.

variants.summary: Moving out is often the riskiest part of leaving. Plan it with an advocate rather than alone.
how: Ask an advocate about shelter options, safe timing, and changing locks.
Ask the police or an advocate whether someone can accompany you to collect belongings.
Keep documents and a packed bag outside the home.
Don’t tell them where you’re going.

steps.title: Untangle the money
steps.summary: Joint accounts and shared bills create reasons to talk. Separate them early.
how: List joint accounts, cards, loans, subscriptions, and who pays each.
Open an account in your name only, with a new login and PIN, and redirect your pay.
Get copies of statements and tax documents. Check your credit report for anything you don’t recognize.
Remove saved payment methods from shared devices and apps.
Get legal or financial advice before closing joint accounts or dividing debts.

steps.title: Get your belongings back once, without a visit
steps.summary: Belongings are the classic excuse for “one more conversation”. Make it a single, boring handoff.
how: Each of you makes a list of what the other has.
Use a third party: a friend, a locker, a drop-off at a neutral place. Agree a day and time in writing.
Let go of low-value things. A few items aren’t worth another round of contact.
If safety is a concern, ask the police or an advocate about an escorted pickup.

steps.title: Switch to low-contact co-parenting
steps.summary: With children, full no contact usually isn’t possible. The aim is contact that is only about them, and as little as possible.
how: Talk only about the children: schedules, health, school. Not the relationship or the past.
Keep it written and short, in an app or email that keeps a record. Some courts require one.
Make the schedule predictable and written. Hand-offs brief and neutral, and never use your child as a messenger.
In high-conflict situations, parallel parenting means each parent runs their own time and you rarely need to coordinate. A mediator or court sets the rules.
At events, sit apart or alternate, and share anything important to the child’s safety or schooling.

scripts.label: A short, neutral reply
scripts.text: Thanks for letting me know. Saturday at 10 works. I’ll drop off at the front desk.

variants.summary: Safety changes the plan. Talk to an advocate and a family lawyer before negotiating anything directly.
how: Ask about supervised or third-party exchanges, and court-ordered communication through an app.
Keep every message on a record-keeping app.
Don’t discuss your location or routine.
Tell the school who is allowed to collect the children.

steps.title: Handle contact at work or school
steps.summary: Work contact is allowed. Make it work-only and unemotional.
how: Stick to work topics, in work channels, in writing where you can.
Be polite and brief. Skip small talk.
If you can, ask for a different team, shift, desk or schedule.
If contact becomes unwelcome or harassing, document it and tell a manager or HR.

scripts.label: Keeping it professional
scripts.text: Happy to talk about the project. I’m not going to discuss anything personal at work.

steps.title: Navigate mutual friends
steps.summary: Friends are a common side door. Be clear without making anyone choose.
how: Ask them not to pass messages or news either way, and not to tell you about the ex.
Don’t ask about them. Skip events they’ll be at for now.
Mute group chats instead of leaving in a huff.
Spend one-on-one time with friends who support you without picking the breakup apart over and over.
Accept that some friendships may cool, and some will deepen.

scripts.label: To a mutual friend
scripts.text: I’m taking a break from contact with them. I’d love to stay close to you, but please don’t pass things between us or tell me what they’re up to.

steps.title: Sort out the pet
steps.summary: Pets are easy to use as a reason to keep talking.
how: Agree ownership or a schedule in writing and keep it simple.
Hand off through a third party. Don’t use the pet as a way to start a conversation.
If safety is a concern, pets can be used as leverage. Include them in your safety plan and ask about pet-friendly shelters.

steps.title: Decide whether to send one final message
steps.summary: You don’t have to. If you do, make it short, clear and final.
how: Three valid options: no message at all, one brief message, or a boundary message only after repeated contact.
If you send one: say what you’re doing, not what they did wrong. No questions, no invitation to reply, no explanations to rebut.
Keep a copy, then block or mute so you aren’t waiting for a reply.
Don’t draft it when you’re hurting. Put it in the unsent box first and sleep on it.

scripts.label: A short final message
scripts.text: I’ve decided to end contact so that I can move forward. Please don’t contact me. I wish you well.

scripts.label: After they keep reaching out
scripts.text: I’ve asked you not to contact me. I won’t be replying to any further messages.

variants.summary: Don’t send anything yet. A message can escalate things.
how: Ask an advocate whether to send anything at all, and when.
If an order is in place, follow its terms and let the court or a lawyer handle any communication.
If you ever do respond, keep it factual and short, and save it.

steps.title: Put the reminders away
steps.summary: Away, not destroyed in a rage. You can decide later what to keep.
how: Move photos and messages to a locked folder, or hand a box to a friend.
Take them off your lock screen and wallpaper, and turn off “memories” features.
Pack gifts and keepsakes in a box out of sight.
Keep anything that could be evidence of harassment, threats or abuse.

steps.title: Expect comeback attempts
steps.summary: Knowing the usual patterns takes away much of their power.
how: Common patterns: an apology with a big promise, sudden warmth or gifts, “accidental” texts, birthday and holiday messages, going through friends, a sudden crisis, or a smear campaign.
They work because they feel hopeful, especially if you’re warm, or the relationship was intense.
Respond neutrally, or not at all. Ask your friends to do the same.
Document everything, and report threats or stalking.

steps.title: Get closure without them
steps.summary: The explanation you’re waiting for may never come, and a final talk rarely delivers it anyway.
how: Write the whole letter, everything you’d say, and don’t send it.
Answer your own questions: what did I need, what did I learn, what would I do differently?
Accept what you can’t change. Acceptance isn’t approval, it just lowers the weight you carry.
Re-read your honest list when you’re missing them.

steps.title: Don’t go back to the bed
steps.summary: A “just once” reunion resets the clock.
how: Sexual reunions complicate healing. One study linked using sex to cope with anger or distress to slower recovery.
Consider a 30-day pause as a minimum.
If you feel tempted, go to the urge toolkit before you reply to anything.

steps.title: Plan for running into them
steps.summary: The first meeting is rough. A default plan makes it manageable.
how: Decide ahead: a neutral nod or hello, then leave. No catching up.
Have an exit line ready and, if you can, your own way home.
Plan something comforting for afterwards.
Seeing them with someone new can hurt. That’s normal and doesn’t mean you should reach out.

scripts.label: An exit line
scripts.text: Hi. I’m just heading out. Take care.

steps.title: If they keep showing up or watching
steps.summary: Repeated unwanted contact isn’t a politeness problem. It may be stalking.
how: Don’t confront them. Write down the date, time and what happened, and save any messages or photos.
Tell trusted people and your employer. Vary your routine.
Report it, and ask an advocate about protective orders and stalking charges where you live.
Check your accounts and devices again for tracking or access.

steps.title: Be careful with a rebound
steps.summary: A new person can feel like relief and still delay the healing.
how: Dating to fill the gap often means carrying the old relationship into the new one.
Reconnect with old friends first and spend some time on your own.
When you do date, go slowly and notice whether the new person respects your boundaries.

steps.title: Rebuild trust in yourself
steps.summary: After a controlling or manipulative relationship, it’s common to doubt your own read on things.
how: Name the pattern. Understanding it makes it less confusing.
Work with a counselor if you can, to spot manipulation and heal.
Practice small decisions and notice they go fine.
Watch how people treat you over time, not just at the start.

steps.title: Friends with an ex someday?
steps.summary: Sometimes, but not as a way back in.
how: Only after a real no-contact stretch, and only if you feel truly fine about their life.
Check your motives: is this friendship, or hope in disguise?
If the relationship was controlling or abusive, friendship probably isn’t a good idea.
